passages.title: The Fourth Measure
passages.topic: a cello student and her little brother
passages.text:
Imani had practiced the same four measures for forty minutes, and each time her bow slid off the note like a boot on ice. The audition was Friday. She pressed her lips together and started again.

From the doorway, her little brother Theo watched with a bowl of cereal. “That was better,” he said.

“It wasn't,” Imani snapped. “Please go away.”

Theo shrugged and wandered off, but he left the door open, and a minute later she heard him in the hall, humming the melody a half step flat. She nearly threw her bow. Instead she grabbed her phone and recorded herself, planning to prove to everyone, mostly to herself, how terrible she sounded.

When she played the recording back, she frowned. The first three measures were steady. The trouble came in the fourth, where her shoulders rose toward her ears and her fingers hurried, as if the music were chasing her. Each time she made a mistake, she stiffened, and the stiffness caused the next mistake.

“So it isn't the notes,” she said aloud.

Theo reappeared, still humming. “Told you.”

“You told me it was better. It wasn't.”

“It was better when you weren't mad,” he said, which was annoyingly specific.

Imani laughed in spite of herself. She set the phone down, rolled her shoulders back, and breathed out slowly before the fourth measure. The note rang clear, warm and round, like a bell. She played it again to be sure it was no accident.

“Okay,” she said. “You can stay. But you have to hum it in tune.”

Theo grinned. “No promises.”

passages.title: Two Entries from Nora's Journal
passages.topic: a new student who finds a club
passages.text:
Monday, September 9

I've decided this town is the quietest place on Earth. Our moving boxes are still stacked in the hall like a cardboard fortress, and the only sound at night is the refrigerator. At my old school I knew everyone's name, and everyone knew mine. Today I ate lunch beside a girl who studied her sandwich as though it held the secrets of the universe. She did not look up once. I counted: nine bites, zero words.

Mom says to give it time. Time, in my experience, is just the thing adults offer when they have no actual solution.

Friday, October 11

Something strange happened. The sandwich girl, whose name is Priya, turns out to run the school's tiny astronomy club, which meets in a supply closet because the real classroom has a leaky ceiling. Yesterday she finally spoke to me. “You keep staring at my notebook,” she said. I had been; she draws planets in the margins with ridiculous precision. I told her so, and she turned bright red and then handed me a spare pencil.

Now I belong to a club of exactly four, and we meet beside mops and a stack of folding chairs. Last night we carried a telescope onto the baseball field, and Priya pointed out Jupiter, a small steady dot with a pale moon beside it. I remembered my count from the first day: nine bites, zero words. Funny how a closet full of mops can turn out to be the loudest place I've ever been.

I'm not saying the town is perfect. But I may have to revise my opinion of the quiet.

passages.title: Eleven Seconds
passages.topic: two partners and a collapsed bridge
passages.text:
The bridge held for eleven seconds. Kenji counted them silently, watching Mr. Alvarez add stack after stack of textbook weights to the center span. At the next stack, there was a crack. A splinter. A sag. Then the whole structure folded in on itself and settled on the table in a heap of glue-stiff sticks.

The gym was quiet except for a few polite claps. Kenji stared at the wreckage. Three weeks of work. He had measured every joint twice and had stayed up on Sunday night to sand the supports smooth. He felt as though someone had pulled out the floor.

“We should have used the triangle pattern,” he muttered. “I knew it. I said it in week one.”

Dara was already kneeling beside the table, holding a broken piece up to the light. “Look at this,” she said. “The break is right here, at the joint, but the sticks aren't even cracked. The glue let go before the wood did.”

“That's worse. That means we messed up.”

“It means we learned which part was weak,” Dara said cheerfully. She flipped open her notebook and began sketching. “If we'd tested it a different way, we might never have known. Now we know exactly what to fix.”

Kenji wanted to stay annoyed, because annoyance felt safer than hope. But Dara's drawing already showed a joint reinforced with a small, paper-thin brace, and he had to admit it looked clever.

“Fine,” he sighed, taking the pencil. “But the triangles are going in, too.”

“Obviously,” Dara said, and handed over the rest of the notebook.

passages.title: Paper Route
passages.text:
The street is a river of gray at six,
and I am the small boat riding it,
my bicycle ticking like a pocket watch,
each house a dock where a porch light waits.
No one is awake to see me pass.

I fold the news into hard white bricks
and toss them, one by one, to sleeping steps.
Thump. Thump. A dog lifts one ear,
decides the world has not yet begun,
and lays it back upon his paws.

My hands are numb; my breath is smoke.
The sky keeps its peach-colored secret
low behind the water tower, patient,
as if it, too, were saving up
a gift for anyone who rises early.

Then the first window glows, gold as a yolk,
and a stranger waves from a kitchen.
I wave back with a cold, bright hand.
Tomorrow I will complain about the dark,
but today I was the first to see the day arrive.

passages.title: The Escape Artists of the Sea
passages.text:
Aquarium keepers often tell stories about octopuses that disappear from their tanks overnight. A loose lid, they say, is an invitation, and a clever octopus will accept it. Behind these stories is real science about how the animals are built and how they think.

The first secret is the octopus's body. It has no bones. Its only hard part is a small, parrot-like beak, and everything else is soft, pliable muscle. Because the beak is the widest rigid piece, an octopus can often pour its body through any opening the beak can fit. A gap that looks far too narrow for a creature of its size may be more than enough.

The second secret is disguise. The octopus's skin contains thousands of tiny pigment sacs called chromatophores. By stretching or squeezing the muscles around these sacs, the animal can change color in moments. It can also raise bumps on its skin to match the texture of rock or coral. In the wild, this lets an octopus seem to vanish against a reef.

The third secret is the octopus's mind. In laboratory tests, octopuses have learned to unscrew jar lids to reach food and to find their way through simple mazes. Much of an octopus's nervous system is spread through its arms, so each arm can explore and react on its own. For an animal this curious, a latch may be a puzzle worth solving.

For this reason, modern aquariums rely on heavy, secure lids and give their octopuses plenty of toys and puzzles to keep busy. Keepers have learned to think like the animal they protect: if its beak fits through, all of it can follow.

passages.title: Why the Sky Changes Color
passages.topic: how sunlight scatters in the atmosphere
passages.text:
On a clear afternoon, the sky seems like a plain blue ceiling. Yet at sunset the same sky may blaze orange and pink. The sky itself has not been repainted. What changes is the path that sunlight takes to reach your eyes.

Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow. Each color travels as a wave of a different length: red light has long waves, and blue light has short ones. When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it collides with gas molecules, tiny bits of air that are much smaller than the light waves. These collisions scatter, or bounce, the light in every direction. Short blue waves are scattered far more strongly than long red waves.

At midday, then, blue light is bounced all across the sky, and wherever you look, some of it is headed toward you. Violet light scatters even more, but the sun gives off less of it and human eyes are less sensitive to it, so the sky appears blue.

At sunrise and sunset, by contrast, the sun sits low on the horizon. Its light must cross a much thicker slice of atmosphere before it reaches you. Along that long route, most of the blue light is scattered out of the beam. What remains are the longer waves, orange and red, which is why the horizon glows with warm color. Dust and tiny droplets in the air can deepen those colors even more.

The blue of noon and the red of evening therefore share a single cause: sunlight sorted by the air it passes through.

passages.title: A Journey No Single Butterfly Finishes
passages.text:
Each fall, monarch butterflies across eastern North America begin a journey south toward the mountain forests of central Mexico. Their paper-thin wings weigh almost nothing, yet the insects can travel thousands of miles to a place they have never seen.

What makes the trip remarkable is that no single butterfly completes the whole yearly circuit. The monarchs that fly south in autumn belong to a special generation that lives for months instead of weeks. When spring arrives, they head north, lay eggs, and die. Their offspring carry on northward, and over several short-lived generations, the monarchs' descendants spread across the continent. By late summer, a new long-lived generation is born, and it turns south again.

This cycle depends on one plant. Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, and females lay their eggs on its leaves. The plant also contains chemicals that make the caterpillars taste unpleasant to many predators, which gives them a measure of protection.

Unfortunately, milkweed has become harder to find. As meadows have been replaced by farms, roads, and neighborhoods, the places where monarchs can raise their young have shrunk, and scientists worry about declining numbers.

The encouraging news is that ordinary people can help. A school yard or backyard garden that includes milkweed for caterpillars and flowers for adult butterflies can serve as a small refuge along the route. A monarch may be tiny, but keeping its journey possible takes many hands, and every garden counts.

passages.title: Give Us Twenty Minutes to Read
passages.topic: a student argues for silent reading time
passages.text:
Every school day, our schedule has room for announcements, locker breaks, and a long lunch, but not a single minute set aside for reading a book of our own choice. That should change. I propose a daily twenty-minute silent reading period for every student at Lakeview Middle School.

First, reading builds skill. Educators have long observed that students who read often tend to know more words and understand harder texts. Twenty minutes a day is short enough to fit into the schedule, yet over a school year it adds up to many hours of practice that most students would not otherwise get.

Second, a quiet reading period would give students a calm break. Our school librarian reports that the library is busiest at lunch, when students arrive looking for something peaceful to do. That suggests many of us want a quieter part of the day.

Third, the evidence from other schools is clear. My cousin's school added a silent reading period last year, and its test scores went up afterward. That proves that the same thing will happen here. Besides, every student who reads for twenty minutes a day will become a straight-A student, and everyone I have talked to agrees with me.

Some people will say we cannot spare the time. But our schedule already includes minutes for activities that matter far less than reading. If it can fit those in, it can fit reading. Lakeview students deserve the chance, and our teachers and librarian deserve a school that values books.

items.prompt: Which detail from the passage best supports the inference that Imani's tension, rather than her skill, is causing her mistakes?
items.answer: She stiffens after each mistake, and that leads to the next one.

wrong.text: She practices the same four measures for forty minutes in a row.
wrong.why: True detail, but it shows effort, not the cause of the mistakes.

wrong.text: Her brother hums the melody a half step flat in the hallway.
wrong.why: Confuses a distraction in the setting with the cause of the errors.

wrong.text: She records herself so she can prove how terrible she sounds.
wrong.why: Shows her attitude, not what actually produces the mistakes.

items.explanation: In paragraph 5, Imani notices that she stiffens after each mistake and that the stiffness causes the next mistake.

items.prompt: In the first paragraph, the simile “like a boot on ice” helps the reader understand that Imani's bow was
items.answer: slipping off the note without gripping the string.

wrong.text: moving too slowly to keep up with the beat.
wrong.why: Misreads ice as meaning slowness instead of lost grip.

wrong.text: producing a harsh, scratchy sound each time.
wrong.why: Assumes the comparison is about sound rather than control.

wrong.text: frozen so that it could not move at all.
wrong.why: Takes the comparison literally instead of noticing that a boot on ice slides.

items.explanation: A boot on ice slides instead of gripping, so the simile shows that the bow keeps slipping off the note.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story about Imani's audition practice?
items.answer: Staying calm can help performance more than forcing harder effort.

wrong.text: Younger siblings often understand music better than older siblings do.
wrong.why: Overgeneralizes from one detail about Theo.

wrong.text: Recording yourself is the best way to prepare for an audition.
wrong.why: Mistakes one step in the plot for the message of the whole story.

wrong.text: Frustration is a sign that a goal is not worth pursuing.
wrong.why: Reverses the lesson; Imani succeeds once she handles her frustration.

items.explanation: Imani plays the fourth measure well only after she relaxes her shoulders and breathes out, not after more forced practice.

items.prompt: How does Theo's remark that it was better “when you weren't mad” affect Imani?
items.answer: It shows her that anger is part of the problem, so she relaxes.

wrong.text: It convinces her that the audition is not very important.
wrong.why: Invents a reaction not supported by the text.

wrong.text: It makes her angrier, so she decides to practice even longer.
wrong.why: Reverses the effect: she relaxes after his comment.

wrong.text: It shows her that Theo understands the cello better than she does.
wrong.why: Overstates Theo's skill; he only notices her mood.

items.explanation: After Theo's comment, Imani laughs, rolls her shoulders back, breathes out, and then plays the note clearly.

items.prompt: How does Theo's view of Imani's playing differ from Imani's own view?
items.answer: Theo sees progress tied to her mood, while Imani judges herself harshly.

wrong.text: Theo thinks she should give up the cello, while Imani wants to keep going.
wrong.why: Invents an opposition the text never shows.

wrong.text: Theo thinks the music is too difficult, while Imani believes it is easy.
wrong.why: Confuses the characters' attitudes toward the piece.

wrong.text: Theo is jealous of her talent, while Imani is proud of her progress.
wrong.why: Assigns emotions to both characters that the text does not state.

items.explanation: Theo says it was better and that it improved when she wasn't mad, while Imani insists it wasn't better and expects to sound terrible.

items.prompt: Which pair of details from the first entry best supports the inference that Nora feels lonely at her new school?
items.answer: She recalls everyone knowing her name and counts zero words at lunch.

wrong.text: She mentions the leaky classroom ceiling and the club's four members.
wrong.why: Details from the second entry that say nothing about her loneliness.

wrong.text: She describes Priya's careful drawings and happily borrows a spare pencil from her.
wrong.why: Details that show friendship forming, not loneliness.

wrong.text: She sees Jupiter through a telescope and notices a pale moon beside it.
wrong.why: True details, but they come after her feelings change.

items.explanation: In the first entry Nora contrasts her old school, where everyone knew her, with a lunch table where no one speaks.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the journal entries?
items.answer: Friendship can form in unexpected places once a person gives things a chance.

wrong.text: Shy people should join clubs so that they never have to eat lunch alone again.
wrong.why: Too narrow and turns the story into advice about lunch.

wrong.text: Adults usually give advice that turns out to be wrong.
wrong.why: Overgeneralizes from Nora's early opinion of her mother.

wrong.text: A new town is always quieter than the town someone left behind.
wrong.why: Focuses on the first impression and ignores how it changes.

items.explanation: Nora begins by judging her town as quiet and lonely, then finds friends in a supply closet and admits she may have to revise her opinion.

items.prompt: How do Priya's actions in the second entry change Nora's view of her new town?
items.answer: Priya's friendly reply gives Nora a group to belong to and softens her opinion.

wrong.text: Priya's embarrassment makes Nora decide that the club is not for her after all.
wrong.why: Reverses the outcome; Nora joins and enjoys the club.

wrong.text: Priya's telescope makes Nora wish she could move back to her old school soon.
wrong.why: Invents a feeling the entry does not mention.

wrong.text: Priya's silence at lunch proves that Nora's first opinion was correct.
wrong.why: Ignores that Priya begins talking and welcomes Nora.

items.explanation: Priya hands Nora a pencil after the compliment, and Nora joins the club and ends the entry ready to revise her opinion of the quiet.

items.prompt: In the second entry, Nora calls a closet full of mops “the loudest place I've ever been.” What does she most likely mean?
items.answer: The closet is full of lively friendship, even though it is small and plain.

wrong.text: The club members argue constantly during their meetings.
wrong.why: Takes loud to mean angry rather than lively.

wrong.text: The closet echoes because it is so small and empty.
wrong.why: Takes the phrase literally as a description of sound.

wrong.text: Nora feels overwhelmed by the noise and wants to leave the club soon.
wrong.why: Misreads her tone, which is warm and amused.

items.explanation: Nora contrasts the quiet town with the energy she finds among friends, so “loud” suggests liveliness rather than noise.

items.prompt: How does the form of two dated journal entries, a month apart, contribute to the meaning of the text?
items.answer: It lets readers compare how Nora feels at the start and the end.

wrong.text: It shows that Nora writes in her journal every single day.
wrong.why: Reads the dates as a habit rather than a structural contrast.

wrong.text: It reveals Priya's private thoughts about the new student.
wrong.why: Confuses a first-person journal with an all-knowing narrator.

wrong.text: It hides the ending so that readers are surprised by Nora's change.
wrong.why: Misses that the structure invites comparison rather than mystery.

items.explanation: The first entry shows Nora lonely and doubtful and the second shows her settled, so the form makes the change easy to see.

items.prompt: Which detail from the passage best supports the inference that Kenji is a careful planner?
items.answer: He measured every joint twice and sanded the supports smooth.

wrong.text: He counted the seconds the bridge held under the growing weights.
wrong.why: Shows attention, but not planning ahead.

wrong.text: He stared at the wreckage after the gym grew quiet.
wrong.why: Shows disappointment, not planning.

wrong.text: He took the pencil from Dara at the end of the scene.
wrong.why: Shows he accepts her idea, not that he plans carefully.

items.explanation: In paragraph 2, Kenji's double-checked measurements and late-night sanding show that he prepares with great care.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story about the bridge?
items.answer: A setback can be useful if it is treated as a chance to learn.

wrong.text: Careful planning always prevents a project from failing.
wrong.why: Contradicts the story, where careful planning still ends in a collapse.

wrong.text: Working with a partner is easier than working alone.
wrong.why: Too general; the story is about how the partners respond to failure.

wrong.text: Glue is a weaker material than wood for building model bridges.
wrong.why: Takes a single detail for the whole message.

items.explanation: Dara uses the collapse to find the weak joint, and Kenji joins in planning a stronger design.

items.prompt: How do Dara's actions after the collapse affect Kenji?
items.answer: Her look at the joint and her sketch move him toward fixing the design.

wrong.text: Her cheerful mood convinces him to leave the triangle pattern out of the design.
wrong.why: Reverses the ending, where he insists on the triangles.

wrong.text: Her notebook proves that he built the joints carelessly.
wrong.why: Misreads her notes as blame rather than information.

wrong.text: Her kneeling at the table causes the teacher to stop the test.
wrong.why: Invents an event that never occurs.

items.explanation: Dara points out that the glue failed first and sketches a reinforcement, and Kenji takes the pencil to join her.

items.prompt: In the first paragraph, the short fragments “A splinter. A sag.” contribute to the passage by
items.answer: breaking the collapse into quick steps that make it feel sudden.

wrong.text: explaining the rules of the bridge contest to the reader in detail.
wrong.why: Misreads a description of action as an explanation.

wrong.text: showing that the narrator is unsure what happened.
wrong.why: Confuses a style choice with uncertainty.

wrong.text: listing the materials that were used to build the bridge.
wrong.why: Mistakes the fragments for a list of supplies.

items.explanation: The abrupt fragments echo the quick stages of the collapse, building tension before the bridge folds.

items.prompt: How do Kenji's and Dara's points of view about the collapse differ?
items.answer: Kenji sees proof of a mistake, while Dara sees what needs repair.

wrong.text: Kenji blames Mr. Alvarez for the test, while Dara blames herself.
wrong.why: Invents blame that is not in the text.

wrong.text: Kenji believes the bridge was a success, while Dara is disappointed.
wrong.why: Reverses their reactions.

wrong.text: Kenji is excited by the failure, while Dara is anxious about it.
wrong.why: Reverses the emotions each character shows.

items.explanation: Kenji says the break means “we messed up,” while Dara says it shows “which part was weak” and begins sketching a fix.

items.prompt: Which details in the fourth stanza best support the inference that the speaker enjoys the early morning despite the cold?
items.answer: The speaker waves back warmly and feels glad to see the day arrive first.

wrong.text: The speaker's hands are numb and the breath looks like smoke in the air.
wrong.why: Details of the cold from stanza 3, not signs of enjoyment.

wrong.text: A dog lifts one ear and then settles back onto his paws.
wrong.why: A detail from stanza 2 that is about the dog, not the speaker's feelings.

wrong.text: The speaker compares the street to a river of gray.
wrong.why: A description from stanza 1 that is not about enjoyment.

items.explanation: In the last stanza the speaker waves back with a “cold, bright hand” and says that today was the first to see the day arrive.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the poem?
items.answer: Ordinary early work can reveal quiet beauty and connection.

wrong.text: Delivering newspapers is harder than most people realize.
wrong.why: Too narrow; the poem celebrates the morning more than the difficulty.

wrong.text: Dogs notice the arrival of morning better than people do.
wrong.why: Builds a theme from a single image.

wrong.text: People who complain about the dark should stop complaining.
wrong.why: Misreads a light joke in the last lines as the poem's lesson.

items.explanation: The speaker finds beauty in the dawn sky and a moment of connection when a stranger waves from a kitchen.

items.prompt: In the second stanza, how does the dog help develop the setting?
items.answer: Its sleepy reaction shows how early and quiet the morning is.

wrong.text: It shows that the speaker is afraid of the neighborhood.
wrong.why: Invents fear that the poem never expresses.

wrong.text: It suggests that the dog's barking will soon wake all the neighbors.
wrong.why: Reverses the detail; the dog goes back to sleep.

wrong.text: It shows that the dog belongs to the speaker.
wrong.why: Assumes a relationship the poem does not mention.

items.explanation: The dog lifts one ear and “decides the world has not yet begun,” which shows how early it is.

items.prompt: In the first stanza, the speaker calls the street “a river of gray” and says, “I am the small boat riding it.” What does this metaphor suggest?
items.answer: The speaker glides quietly through the dim early light.

wrong.text: The speaker is lost and drifting in a flooded neighborhood.
wrong.why: Takes the metaphor literally and adds danger.

wrong.text: The speaker is rowing hard against a strong current.
wrong.why: Imports an effort that the image does not suggest.

wrong.text: The speaker is leaving the town to travel by water.
wrong.why: Confuses the comparison with an actual boat trip.

items.explanation: Comparing the street to a river and the speaker to a small boat suggests smooth, quiet travel through the gray light.

items.prompt: How does the word “Then” at the start of the final stanza contribute to the poem's meaning?
items.answer: It marks a shift from dark and quiet to light and human connection.

wrong.text: It shows that the speaker plans to quit the paper route before winter.
wrong.why: Misreads the speaker's last lines as a decision.

wrong.text: It repeats the first stanza to show that nothing has changed.
wrong.why: Ignores the new images of light and the stranger's wave.

wrong.text: It introduces a new speaker who responds to the first one.
wrong.why: Confuses a shift in the scene with a change of speaker.

items.explanation: Until the last stanza the street is dark and empty, and “Then” introduces a glowing window and a friendly wave.

items.prompt: According to the passage, which detail best supports the claim that an octopus's body helps it escape?
items.answer: Its only hard part is a beak, so it can pour through any gap the beak fits.

wrong.text: It can change color within moments by moving the muscles around its pigment sacs.
wrong.why: True, but this supports the claim about disguise, not the body's shape.

wrong.text: It has learned to unscrew jar lids to reach food in laboratory tests.
wrong.why: Evidence of intelligence, not body structure.

wrong.text: Aquarium keepers tell stories about octopuses that vanish overnight.
wrong.why: Shows that escapes happen, not why the body allows them.

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that the beak is the widest rigid part, so the soft body can follow it through narrow gaps.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
items.answer: An octopus's soft body, disguise, and intelligence make it a skilled escape artist.

wrong.text: Octopuses can change color to match their surroundings in a matter of moments.
wrong.why: Too narrow; covers only one section.

wrong.text: Octopuses are the smartest animals in the ocean.
wrong.why: Overgeneralizes beyond what the passage claims.

wrong.text: Aquariums should stop keeping octopuses in tanks.
wrong.why: An opinion that the passage does not make.

items.explanation: The passage presents three “secrets” (body, disguise, mind) that explain the escapes.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, how does the author connect the octopus's beak to its ability to escape?
items.answer: The beak is the widest hard part, so it limits the gaps the body can pass.

wrong.text: The beak lets the octopus unscrew jar lids and open latches.
wrong.why: Confuses the beak with the arms, which the passage links to exploring.

wrong.text: The beak is so large that it prevents the octopus from squeezing out of tanks.
wrong.why: Reverses the idea that a small beak allows passage.

wrong.text: The beak changes color so the octopus can hide in the gap.
wrong.why: Mixes up the beak with the pigment sacs in the skin.

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the beak is the widest rigid piece, so if it fits through, the soft body can follow.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2, the author describes the octopus's body as “soft, pliable muscle.” The word “pliable” most nearly means
items.answer: easily bent or shaped.

wrong.text: strong and heavy for its size.
wrong.why: Associates muscle with strength instead of using the context of squeezing through gaps.

wrong.text: wet and slippery.
wrong.why: Confuses the animal's habitat with the quality described.

wrong.text: hard to see.
wrong.why: Mixes up this word with the later discussion of disguise.

items.explanation: The sentence says the octopus can pour through a narrow gap, so its muscle must bend easily.

items.prompt: How does the first paragraph contribute to the development of the passage?
items.answer: It introduces the puzzle of escapes, which later paragraphs explain.

wrong.text: It traces the history of aquariums and the animals they keep.
wrong.why: Mistakes a hook about keepers' stories for a history.

wrong.text: It argues that octopuses are dangerous animals to keep.
wrong.why: Imports a warning the passage never gives.

wrong.text: It summarizes the conclusion about how keepers protect their octopuses.
wrong.why: Confuses the introduction with the closing paragraph.

items.explanation: The opening describes the stories and says real science lies behind them; the body paragraphs then supply the explanation.

items.prompt: Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that the sky's color depends on the path of sunlight?
items.answer: At sunset, light crosses thicker air that scatters out blue, leaving orange and red.

wrong.text: Sunlight looks white but is a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow.
wrong.why: True, but it explains the light's makeup, not the path it takes.

wrong.text: Violet light scatters even more strongly than blue light does, though the sun gives off less of it.
wrong.why: A detail about colors, not about the path of the light.

wrong.text: Dust and tiny droplets can deepen the colors near the horizon.
wrong.why: A supporting detail, not the main evidence for the claim.

items.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that a low sun sends light through more atmosphere, which removes blue and leaves warmer colors.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
items.answer: The sky's colors come from how air scatters the colors of sunlight.

wrong.text: Dust in the air is the main reason sunsets are colorful.
wrong.why: Too narrow; dust only deepens the colors.

wrong.text: The sky is blue because it reflects the color of the ocean.
wrong.why: A common misconception that the passage does not support.

wrong.text: White sunlight is made of many colors, each traveling as a wave of its own length.
wrong.why: A supporting detail rather than the main idea.

items.explanation: The passage explains that scattering sorts the colors, producing a blue sky at midday and warm colors at sunset.

items.prompt: According to the passage, how does the position of the sun at sunset affect the blue light that reaches your eyes?
items.answer: A low sun sends light through more air, so more blue is scattered away.

wrong.text: A low sun sends out less light, so every color fades by the same amount.
wrong.why: Ignores that colors are affected differently.

wrong.text: A low sun causes red light to scatter more strongly than blue.
wrong.why: Reverses the relationship between wave length and scattering.

wrong.text: A low sun lets blue light travel straight to the viewer.
wrong.why: Reverses the effect of the longer path.

items.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the long path through thick atmosphere scatters out most of the blue light.

items.prompt: In paragraph 1, the phrase “blaze orange and pink” suggests that the sunset sky is
items.answer: intensely bright and glowing.

wrong.text: dangerously hot to the touch.
wrong.why: Takes blaze literally as fire.

wrong.text: slowly fading into darkness.
wrong.why: Confuses the sunset's end with its color.

wrong.text: patchy and uneven across the horizon.
wrong.why: Introduces a detail not suggested by the word.

items.explanation: “Blaze” has a connotation of bright, strong light, so it describes vivid colors.

items.prompt: How do paragraphs 3 and 4 relate to each other?
items.answer: Paragraph 3 explains the blue midday sky, and paragraph 4 contrasts it with sunset.

wrong.text: Paragraph 3 describes a problem with the sky, and paragraph 4 offers its solution.
wrong.why: Applies the wrong text structure.

wrong.text: Both paragraphs describe how the sky looks at sunset.
wrong.why: Misses that paragraph 3 is about midday.

wrong.text: Paragraph 4 shows that the idea in paragraph 3 is false.
wrong.why: Confuses a contrast with a contradiction.

items.explanation: Paragraph 3 covers midday light, and paragraph 4 begins “at sunrise and sunset, by contrast.”

items.prompt: Which detail from the passage best supports the claim that no single monarch completes the whole yearly journey?
items.answer: The spring monarchs lay eggs and die, and their offspring continue the trip.

wrong.text: Monarchs fly toward the mountain forests of central Mexico each fall season.
wrong.why: Describes the destination, not who completes the trip.

wrong.text: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed leaves.
wrong.why: True, but unrelated to who finishes the journey.

wrong.text: The monarch's wings are paper-thin and weigh almost nothing.
wrong.why: A true detail about the butterfly, not about the cycle.

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that the spring travelers die after laying eggs and later generations carry on.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
items.answer: Monarch migration relies on several generations and on milkweed, so people can help it continue.

wrong.text: Monarchs are the only butterflies in North America that make such a long migration.
wrong.why: Overgeneralizes; the passage does not compare monarchs to others.

wrong.text: Milkweed is poisonous to nearly every animal that eats it.
wrong.why: Distorts the passage's detail about caterpillar protection.

wrong.text: Farms and roads are the only reason monarchs are declining.
wrong.why: Too narrow and too absolute.

items.explanation: The passage explains the generational cycle and the need for milkweed, then ends with how people can help.

items.prompt: According to the passage, how are monarch caterpillars connected to milkweed?
items.answer: Females lay eggs on it, and caterpillars eat it and gain some protection.

wrong.text: The caterpillars carry milkweed seeds south with them when they migrate each fall.
wrong.why: Invents a role that the passage never mentions.

wrong.text: Milkweed supplies the nectar that adult butterflies need.
wrong.why: Confuses caterpillar food with the flowers adults feed on.

wrong.text: The caterpillars harm milkweed, so scientists remove the plants.
wrong.why: Contradicts the passage's call to plant more milkweed.

items.explanation: Paragraph 3 says caterpillars eat only milkweed, females lay eggs on it, and its chemicals help protect the young.

items.prompt: In paragraph 1, the author describes the monarchs' “paper-thin wings.” This phrase suggests that the wings are
items.answer: delicate and easily damaged.

wrong.text: plain and lacking in color.
wrong.why: Confuses thin with dull.

wrong.text: fast enough to outrun predators.
wrong.why: Draws on weight and ignores the connotation of fragility.

wrong.text: worthless to the insect.
wrong.why: Reads paper as something to throw away.

items.explanation: “Paper-thin” suggests fragility, which makes the long journey seem more remarkable.

items.prompt: What is the author's main purpose in the last two paragraphs?
items.answer: To encourage readers to help monarchs by planting milkweed and flowers.

wrong.text: To prove that monarchs are the fastest migrating insects in the world.
wrong.why: Mistakes a detail for the author's purpose.

wrong.text: To warn readers that gardens harm migrating butterflies.
wrong.why: Reverses the author's point of view.

wrong.text: To explain how scientists tag butterflies to follow them.
wrong.why: Imports a topic not found in the passage.

items.explanation: The author describes the loss of milkweed and then says ordinary people can help, with gardens that include milkweed and flowers.

items.prompt: Which claim in the passage is NOT supported by sufficient evidence?
items.answer: Because the cousin's school saw scores rise, the same will happen at Lakeview.

wrong.text: Students who read often tend to know more words.
wrong.why: A general observation offered by educators; reasonable support.

wrong.text: Twenty minutes a day adds up to many hours of practice over a whole school year.
wrong.why: Sound reasoning from simple arithmetic.

wrong.text: The library is busiest at lunch, according to the librarian.
wrong.why: Specific evidence from a relevant source.

items.explanation: One school's results do not prove what will happen at another, and the author gives no other evidence for the claim.

items.prompt: Which describes the flaw in the author's reasoning about the cousin's school in paragraph 4?
items.answer: It assumes the reading period caused the scores and ignores other reasons.

wrong.text: It uses an example from a school that is too far away to be a fair comparison.
wrong.why: The text says the change happened last year.

wrong.text: It attacks the people who disagree instead of their ideas.
wrong.why: The paragraph does not criticize opponents.

wrong.text: It relies on an expert who is never named, so readers cannot check the claim.
wrong.why: The paragraph names a relative, not an expert.

items.explanation: The paragraph treats scores that rose afterward as proof of cause, without considering other changes at that school.

items.prompt: Which evidence does the author give to support the idea that many students want a quieter part of the day?
items.answer: The librarian reports that the library is busiest at lunch.

wrong.text: Educators observe that frequent readers know more words.
wrong.why: Evidence about skill, not about wanting quiet.

wrong.text: The schedule includes announcements, locker breaks, and a long lunch.
wrong.why: A detail from the opening, not evidence of what students want.

wrong.text: The author's cousin attends a school with a reading period.
wrong.why: Evidence offered for test scores, not quiet.

items.explanation: In paragraph 3 the author cites the librarian's report that students crowd the library at lunch.

items.prompt: How does the last paragraph contribute to the development of the argument?
items.answer: It answers a concern about lost time, which strengthens the author's position.

wrong.text: It drops the original proposal and suggests a different idea for the schedule.
wrong.why: The last paragraph defends the original proposal.

wrong.text: It repeats the introduction without adding any new point.
wrong.why: Misses the counterclaim that the paragraph answers.

wrong.text: It lists the schedule changes the school has already approved.
wrong.why: No approval is mentioned in the passage.

items.explanation: The author raises the objection that there is no time and replies that the schedule already fits less important activities.

items.prompt: Which detail best shows that the author is writing from the perspective of a student?
items.answer: The author refers to “our schedule” and to what “many of us want.”

wrong.text: The author cites a report from the school librarian about the busy library.
wrong.why: Citing a librarian does not show the author's own role.

wrong.text: The author mentions what educators have observed.
wrong.why: This reports others' views, not the author's own.

wrong.text: The author proposes a rule for every classroom.
wrong.why: A teacher or student could make that proposal.

items.explanation: Words such as “our” and “us” show that the author is a member of the student body.

items.prompt: The hikers were famished after the long climb, so they devoured everything in their packs. What does “famished” mean?
items.answer: extremely hungry

wrong.text: very tired and sore
wrong.why: Picks the feeling usually linked to a long climb instead of using the clue 'devoured.'

wrong.text: very cold and wet
wrong.why: Draws on the outdoor setting instead of the context.

wrong.text: quite proud of it
wrong.why: Chooses a feeling about the climb, not about eating.

items.explanation: Because they devoured everything they had packed, “famished” must mean very hungry.

items.prompt: The Latin root “aqua” means “water,” and “duct” comes from a word meaning “to lead.” An aqueduct is most likely a structure that
items.answer: carries water to other places

wrong.text: stores water for a town in a tank.
wrong.why: Ignores the meaning of 'lead' and picks storage.

wrong.text: removes salt from sea water.
wrong.why: Confuses the root with water treatment.

wrong.text: measures how much rain has fallen.
wrong.why: Connects water to weather, not to leading.

items.explanation: “Aqua” (water) and “duct” (lead) together suggest a channel that leads water elsewhere.

items.prompt: After the storm, the river rose past its banks and flooded the road. Which meaning of “banks” fits this sentence?
items.answer: land along a river's edge

wrong.text: places where money is kept
wrong.why: Picks the most common meaning without using context.

wrong.text: rows of switches or controls
wrong.why: Picks an unrelated meaning of the same word.

wrong.text: turns made by an airplane
wrong.why: Picks a different meaning that does not fit a river.

items.explanation: The river overflowing its “banks” points to the land at the river's edge.

items.prompt: A sign warned that the road was impassable after the flood. Using the prefix “im-” (not) and the suffix “-able” (can be done), what does “impassable” mean?
items.answer: cannot be traveled

wrong.text: easy to travel
wrong.why: Ignores the meaning of the prefix.

wrong.text: recently repaired
wrong.why: Reads the sign's warning as good news.

wrong.text: open only at night
wrong.why: Invents a condition not suggested by the parts.

items.explanation: “Im-” means not, and “passable” means able to be passed, so the road cannot be traveled.

items.prompt: Her rambling speech was so verbose that the audience began checking their watches. What does “verbose” mean?
items.answer: using more words than needed

wrong.text: speaking much too quietly to hear
wrong.why: Chooses a speech problem that would not make people check watches.

wrong.text: filled with strong emotion
wrong.why: Misreads rambling as emotional.

wrong.text: carefully practiced
wrong.why: Picks a positive trait that the context contradicts.

items.explanation: The audience grows bored by a rambling speech, so verbose means wordy.

items.prompt: The Latin prefix “retro-” means “back,” and the root “spect” means “to look.” In retrospect, the team realized it should have practiced more. What does “in retrospect” mean?
items.answer: when looking back at the past

wrong.text: when planning for the future ahead
wrong.why: Reverses the direction of the prefix.

wrong.text: when watching the game closely
wrong.why: Uses only the root and ignores the prefix.

wrong.text: when making a quick decision
wrong.why: Picks a meaning unrelated to either part.

items.explanation: “Retro-” (back) plus “spect” (look) gives the meaning looking back.

items.prompt: The scientist wanted a sound explanation, not a guess. Which meaning of “sound” fits this sentence?
items.answer: based on good reasoning

wrong.text: a noise that can be heard
wrong.why: Picks the most common meaning.

wrong.text: in good physical health
wrong.why: Picks another meaning of the word that does not fit.

wrong.text: a narrow stretch of water
wrong.why: Picks a rare meaning unrelated to explanations.

items.explanation: An explanation contrasted with a guess must be well reasoned and reliable.

items.prompt: The committee had hoped for a swift decision, but the debate dragged on, and members grew weary of the protracted meeting. What does “protracted” mean?
items.answer: lasting longer than expected

wrong.text: filled with angry arguments
wrong.why: Assumes a debate means anger; the clue is 'dragged on.'

wrong.text: held in a private room
wrong.why: Invents a detail not in the sentence.

wrong.text: attended by only a few members
wrong.why: Misreads weary members as missing members.

items.explanation: Contrasted with a swift decision, a meeting that drags on is protracted, meaning drawn out.

items.prompt: When Jo heard that her best friend was moving away, she was down in the dumps. What does the idiom “down in the dumps” mean?
items.answer: sad and discouraged

wrong.text: angry at her friend
wrong.why: Confuses sadness with anger.

wrong.text: sick to her stomach
wrong.why: Reads the idiom as describing a physical illness.

wrong.text: embarrassed in public
wrong.why: Misses the emotional meaning of the news.

items.explanation: Hearing that a friend is leaving makes Jo feel sad, which is what “down in the dumps” means.

items.prompt: The town's new fire station burned down on its opening day. What makes this situation ironic?
items.answer: A building meant to fight fires was itself destroyed by one.

wrong.text: Fires happen often in towns that have many new buildings.
wrong.why: Offers a general fact instead of an unexpected contrast.

wrong.text: Opening days are usually very busy times for the firefighters.
wrong.why: Describes something expected, not ironic.

wrong.text: Fire stations are usually built of brick, not wood.
wrong.why: Invents a detail unrelated to the contrast.

items.explanation: Irony is a result that is the opposite of what is expected, and a fire station is expected to be safe from fire.

items.prompt: “After the substitute left, the classroom was a zoo.” What does this metaphor mean?
items.answer: The room was noisy and out of control.

wrong.text: The room was full of animals.
wrong.why: Takes the metaphor literally.

wrong.text: The room was crowded with visitors.
wrong.why: Confuses a zoo with a crowd of visitors.

wrong.text: The room was carefully organized by the students.
wrong.why: Misses the meaning of wild disorder.

items.explanation: Calling a room a zoo suggests loud, wild behavior.

items.prompt: “Hot” is to “scorching” as “cold” is to which word?
items.answer: freezing

wrong.text: cool
wrong.why: Picks a weaker degree and misses the relationship of intensity.

wrong.text: winter weather
wrong.why: Picks something related to cold rather than a stronger degree.

wrong.text: snow
wrong.why: Picks a related thing, not an intensified word.

items.explanation: Scorching is a stronger form of hot, and freezing is a stronger form of cold.

items.prompt: Mara praised her uncle for being ___ with money, because he always saved for the things he needed. Which word has the most positive connotation?
items.answer: thrifty

wrong.text: stingy
wrong.why: Has the same basic meaning but a negative connotation.

wrong.text: miserly
wrong.why: Suggests greed and does not fit praise.

wrong.text: greedy
wrong.why: Suggests wanting more than one's share, which does not fit.

items.explanation: All the words relate to saving money, but only “thrifty” sounds like praise.

items.prompt: Dani decided to bite the bullet and tell her coach about the injury. What does the idiom “bite the bullet” mean here?
items.answer: do something hard she had been avoiding

wrong.text: speak angrily to someone in charge of the team
wrong.why: Confuses a tough action with an angry one.

wrong.text: hurt herself on purpose
wrong.why: Reads the idiom literally.

wrong.text: ask for help from a teammate
wrong.why: Picks a plausible action not suggested by the idiom.

items.explanation: “Bite the bullet” means to face an unpleasant task, such as admitting an injury.

items.prompt: “The old truck coughed and wheezed up the hill.” What does this figure of speech show?
items.answer: The truck struggled, making sounds like someone out of breath.

wrong.text: The truck's driver was sick with a cold and was coughing in the cab.
wrong.why: Reads the figure of speech literally.

wrong.text: The truck was moving quickly and quietly.
wrong.why: Reverses the effect of the coughing and wheezing.

wrong.text: The truck had just been repaired.
wrong.why: Invents a fact not suggested by the sentence.

items.explanation: Personification gives the truck human sounds of coughing and wheezing to show strain.

items.prompt: Before voting, council members chose to ___ the survey data to decide which pattern mattered most. Which word best completes the sentence?
items.answer: analyze

wrong.text: recite
wrong.why: Picks a word about repeating rather than examining.

wrong.text: conceal
wrong.why: Picks a word that is opposite to using data.

wrong.text: dispute
wrong.why: Picks a word about arguing rather than studying.

items.explanation: To analyze data means to examine its parts to find patterns.

items.prompt: The scientist's findings were ___ because three independent teams repeated the experiment and got the same results. Which word best completes the sentence?
items.answer: consistent

wrong.text: coincidental
wrong.why: Misreads agreement among teams as chance.

wrong.text: vague
wrong.why: Picks a word that conflicts with clear repeated results.

wrong.text: unprecedented
wrong.why: Picks an impressive-sounding word that does not fit.

items.explanation: Results that match across repeated trials are consistent.

items.prompt: The twins looked alike, but their personalities were ___: one was talkative and the other quiet. Which word best completes the sentence?
items.answer: contrasting

wrong.text: exactly identical
wrong.why: Ignores the 'but' signal in the sentence.

wrong.text: very similar
wrong.why: Picks the word that matches the twins' appearance.

wrong.text: equal
wrong.why: Picks a word about amount, not difference.

items.explanation: A talkative twin and a quiet twin have contrasting personalities.

items.prompt: Ana saw wet umbrellas by the door and inferred that it had been raining. What does “inferred” mean?
items.answer: figured out from clues, not told

wrong.text: heard from someone who had been outside
wrong.why: Confuses an inference with being told.

wrong.text: hoped would happen soon
wrong.why: Confuses an inference with a wish.

wrong.text: remembered from an earlier day
wrong.why: Confuses reasoning with memory.

items.explanation: Ana reasoned from the clue of wet umbrellas, which is what it means to infer.

items.prompt: Before the experiment, Leo wrote a hypothesis: “Plants given more light will grow taller.” What is a hypothesis?
items.answer: a testable prediction about what might happen

wrong.text: a final result that has already been proven true
wrong.why: Confuses a prediction with a conclusion.

wrong.text: a list of materials for an experiment
wrong.why: Confuses a hypothesis with a materials list.

wrong.text: a personal opinion that cannot be tested
wrong.why: Ignores that a hypothesis can be tested.

items.explanation: Leo's statement can be tested by growing plants in different amounts of light.
